Why the plate corner broke off

NACS wall holder, the print of September 19, dropped on the floor on October 10. The first two pictures come from the print file as it was (the revision used the same plate, pads and slicer recipe), not from a sketch; the last two from the fixed file.

The base plate is 3/16 in thick, but it is not solid. The slicer prints it as two skins of three layers (about 1/32 in each) over a 20% gyroid core, with three walls around the edge. The only solid plastic is the pad around each screw, 1/2 in in radius. Everything else inside the plate is open lattice, so a corner that hits the floor is a thin hollow flap with a half-depth countersink through it.

The numbers

FeatureAs printedWhy it matters
Plate thickness3/16 inTwo 1/32 in skins carry all the bending; the core only spaces them
Core between the skins20% gyroid, 1/8 in thickShears and crushes under a corner hit; a break face here looks hollow
Walls at the plate edge3 loops, about 5/64 inThe only solid plastic along the edge outside the pads
Solid pad around each screw1/2 in radiusProtects the ring around the hole, not the flap's root along the edge (about 7/8 in of edge per corner is unprotected)
Countersink3/32 in deep, half the plateHalves the section at the hole, and the drum blend lands on its edge
Material and layersPETG Basic, 0.30 mm layers, plate downLayers lie in the plate's plane; a drop bends the corner across them, which the skins resist well but the lattice does not

What that means

A drop onto a corner puts the whole holder's momentum into one flap of plate. The two thin skins have to take the bending on their own, with a half-depth countersink and the drum's blend both landing on the same line. Once the skins crack, the lattice core has nothing to offer, so the corner comes away clean. The screw pads kept the ring around the hole solid, and nothing else.

Where it broke, and the fix Brian: it broke along the contour of the main cylinder, so the flap came off at its root around the drum's blend. His pick: both fixes, a solid plate and a thicker one.

After the fix

The plate is now 1/4 in thick, and the print file makes the whole plate solid, plus a ring up through the drum's blend, so the flap's root is solid plastic from the wall to above the blend. Same slicer recipe otherwise. Both pictures below come from the new print file and the new STL.

The ring Studio shows

Brian, October 11: the added ring is squared off, it should round into the wall plate the way the drum rounds into the flange. That ring is not plastic. It is the slicer's modifier, the region told to print solid, and Bambu Studio draws a modifier translucent over the part. The first version was a squared-off ring that poked out of the blend, and it showed through the screw holes and on the plate's top too. The printed part was always the body on the right, blend and all. The modifier now follows the blend's arc from 0.6 mm inside it, stops a layer under the plate's top, and stays clear of the screw holes, so it sits wholly inside the body and Studio shows the part as it prints.

The face, solid too

Brian, October 11: the face should also be solid infill, like the base; it will also break if dropped. A second modifier now makes the flange, the lip and the blend behind the flange print solid. The model builds it itself, so it follows the lip's rounded edges, keeps 0.6 mm inside every face, stays 0.6 mm under the floors of the T, the wordmark and the frame line, and clears the mouth and its rounded rim. None of it lies outside the body.
